chapters.title: Chapter 1: What a Central Bank Actually Does

lessons.title: Inflation Targeting in India: The 4% Target and the 2 to 6% Band

body.text: An inflation target is a promise with a number on it. By committing to 4%, with a hard floor of 2% and ceiling of 6%, the RBI gives every household, business and bond investor in India a price level they can plan around, and gives the public a clear test of whether the central bank is doing its job.

children.text: You now know who sets rates and what the law asks of them. This lesson unpacks the single number at the centre of it all: the 4% inflation target. Where it came from, why it is 4% and not 2%, what happens when the RBI misses it, and how to use it to read where interest rates are heading.
Why India Needed a Number

markDefs.definition: Getting households and businesses to believe inflation will stay near a known level, so that wage demands, price setting and interest rates stop building in fears of runaway inflation.

children.text: In 2012-13 and 2013-14, consumer inflation in India ran close to 10% a year. FD rates looked attractive on paper but savers were losing money after inflation, and households rushed into gold and real estate to protect themselves. The problem was not just high inflation. It was that nobody knew what the RBI was aiming for, so nobody could plan. Economists call the fix
anchoring inflation expectations

If people believe inflation will stay near 4%, workers ask for raises built around 4%, companies set prices around 4%, and lenders price loans around 4%. The belief itself helps keep inflation there. A clear, public, legally binding target is how a central bank earns that belief.

body.title: How India's Inflation Target Was Built

events.title: Urjit Patel Committee report
events.description: An RBI expert committee recommended flexible inflation targeting: a 4% CPI target with a band of plus or minus 2%, a monetary policy committee, and a switch from wholesale prices (WPI) to consumer prices (CPI) as the main measure.

events.title: Monetary Policy Framework Agreement
events.description: The RBI and the Ministry of Finance signed an agreement committing the RBI to a CPI inflation objective.

events.title: Target becomes law
events.description: After the RBI Act was amended, the government formally notified the 4% target with the 2% to 6% band for the period up to March 2021.

events.title: First renewal
events.description: The same target and band were retained for April 2021 to March 2026.

events.title: RBI reopens the debate
events.description: The RBI published a discussion paper asking whether to target headline or core inflation, whether 4% was still right, and whether the band should change.

events.title: New CPI series
events.description: MoSPI launched a revised CPI with base year 2024, a larger basket, and a lower weight for food.

events.title: Second renewal
events.description: The government retained the 4% target and 2% to 6% band on headline CPI for April 2026 to March 2031.

markDefs.definition: The range around the inflation target within which inflation is considered acceptable, allowing for temporary shocks that monetary policy cannot control in the short run.

children.text: The band exists because monetary policy cannot fine-tune inflation month by month. A poor monsoon can send tomato and onion prices soaring within weeks, and no repo rate change can grow more tomatoes. The
tolerance band
gives the RBI room to look through temporary shocks, while the 4% midpoint tells everyone where it wants inflation to settle over time.

body.text: A common misreading: the band does not mean the RBI is happy anywhere between 2% and 6%. The target is 4%. Inflation sitting at 5.8% for months is inside the band but well above target, and the MPC will act on that. The band edges are failure lines, not comfort zones.

children.text: Why 4% and Not 2% Like the US?
The US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Bank of England all target 2%. India chose a higher number for sound reasons:
Food is a big part of the basket.

Even after the 2026 revision, food and beverages carry about 37% of CPI weight in India, far higher than in developed economies. Food prices swing sharply with weather, which makes a very low target hard to hold.
A fast-growing economy sees faster price change.
As incomes rise, prices of services such as healthcare, education and housing tend to rise faster, especially in a country catching up with richer ones.
Too low a target can choke growth.
Forcing inflation down to 2% in India would likely need very high real interest rates, which would slow lending and job creation.

body.title: Quick Check: Reading the Band
body.question: CPI inflation has averaged 5.6% for the last two quarters. Which statement is correct?
options: The RBI has failed its mandate because inflation is above 4%
Inflation is inside the band, but above target, so the MPC is likely to lean towards tighter policy
The RBI has no reason to act until inflation crosses 6%
The government must now change the target to 6%
body.explanation: Inflation between 2% and 6% is not a legal failure, so the first option is wrong. But the target is 4%, not "anything under 6%", so the MPC will be concerned about inflation running 1.6 percentage points above target and will lean towards holding or raising rates. The target can only be changed by the government through a formal notification, not because of two quarters of data.

children.text: Headline or Core? The Debate India Just Settled

markDefs.definition: Inflation measured across the full CPI basket, including volatile items such as food and fuel.
Inflation excluding food and fuel, which tends to be more stable and more responsive to interest rates.

children.text: The target uses
headline inflation
, the full CPI basket. Some economists argue the RBI should target
core inflation
instead, because interest rates have little effect on food and fuel prices in the short run. The RBI's 2025 discussion paper put this question to the public.

body.title: Headline vs Core Inflation as the Target

columns.label: Target headline CPI
points: Measures what households actually pay, including food and fuel
Easy for the public to understand and verify
Food price spikes feed into wages and expectations over time
Harder for the RBI to control in any single quarter

columns.label: Target core CPI
points: Strips out food and fuel, which rates cannot directly influence
More stable, so easier to steer with interest rates
Could look fine while households struggle with food costs
Risks losing public trust in the target

children.text: In March 2026 the government kept headline CPI as the target. The logic is simple: in a country where food takes such a large share of household budgets, a target that ignores food would not feel credible to most people.
What Counts as Failure
The law does not judge the RBI on a single month. The test uses quarterly averages, and a failure is declared only if the average stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters.

body.caption: Each π is the year-on-year CPI inflation rate for that month

body.title: Name the Trigger
body.textWithBlank: The RBI must send a report to the government if average inflation stays above 6% or below 2% for three consecutive ___.
body.explanation: Quarters, not months. Using three-month averages over three consecutive quarters, nine months in all, stops a single bad monsoon month from triggering a failure while still holding the RBI to account for persistent misses.

children.text: When a failure happens, Section 45ZN of the RBI Act requires the RBI to send the government a report with three things: why the target was missed, what it will do to fix it, and how long it expects to take.
Case 1: The First Failure, 2022

events.title: Above the ceiling
events.description: CPI inflation crossed 6% and stayed above it, driven by food prices and then the global commodity spike after the Russia-Ukraine war began in February.

events.title: Off-cycle hike
events.description: The MPC raised the repo rate by 40 basis points at an unscheduled meeting, starting a cycle that took the rate from 4.00% to 6.50% by February 2023.

events.title: Third quarter confirmed
events.description: CPI inflation was 7.41% in September, locking in three straight quarters above 6%: January to March, April to June and July to September 2022.

events.title: Special MPC meeting
events.description: For the first time since 2016, the MPC met specifically to draft its failure report to the government under Section 45ZN.

body.text: The failure report did not come with a penalty. Its power is accountability: the RBI has to put its reasoning and its plan in writing. The 250 basis points of hikes that followed were the real response. Inflation took time to settle: it dipped below 6% in 2023, jumped above 7% in July 2023 on a vegetable price spike, and only moved back inside the band on a sustained basis after that.

children.text: Case 2: The Near Miss on the Low Side, 2025-26

Most people assume the RBI only worries about high inflation. In 2025, India tested the other edge of the band. A bumper harvest, falling vegetable prices and GST rate cuts in September 2025 pulled inflation to a record low of 0.25% in October 2025.

body.title: Monthly CPI Inflation vs the Tolerance Band (%)

children.text: Now apply the failure test using quarterly averages for 2025-26:

body.title: Calculate the Q3 Average
body.prompt: Using the monthly figures in the table, what was the average CPI inflation rate for October to December 2025? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: (0.25 + 0.71 + 1.33) ÷ 3 = 2.29 ÷ 3 = 0.76%. That is well below 2%, making Q3 the second consecutive quarter under the lower band. But Q4 averaged 3.12%, back inside the band, so the streak stopped at two quarters and no failure was declared.

body.text: The chart joins two CPI series. Figures up to December 2025 use the old base year 2012, and figures from January 2026 use the new base year 2024. Year-on-year comparisons across the switch are indicative, not perfectly like for like.

body.title: Why Would the RBI Worry About Low Inflation?
body.scenario: It is November 2025. CPI inflation has just printed 0.25%. A friend says, "This is great news, prices are barely rising. Why is anyone talking about the RBI failing?"
body.prompt: Explain to your friend why inflation far below 2% can be a problem, and what the MPC did about it.
body.modelAnswer: Very low inflation is not automatically good. First, real interest rates shoot up: with the repo rate at 5.50% and inflation at 0.25%, the policy rate measured against actual inflation was above 5%, which is very tight and discourages borrowing and investment. Second, if low inflation reflects collapsing food prices, farmers' incomes suffer, which hurts rural demand. Third, if people start expecting prices to stay flat or fall, they postpone purchases, which slows the economy further. The MPC responded by cutting the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.25% in December 2025, and one member even argued for an accommodative stance. The low-side band exists precisely so the RBI is held accountable for inflation that is too low, not just too high.

children.text: The Real Interest Rate: Using the Target Like an Analyst

markDefs.definition: The interest rate after subtracting inflation. It shows the true cost of borrowing and the true return on saving.

children.text: The inflation target becomes truly useful when you combine it with the repo rate. The difference between them is the
real interest rate
, and it tells you how tight or loose policy really is.

body.caption: Analysts usually use the RBI's own inflation projection for the next four quarters

body.title: How Tight Is Policy Right Now?
body.prompt: After its August 2026 meeting, the RBI kept the repo rate at 5.25% and projected CPI inflation of 5.0% for 2026-27. What is the approximate real policy rate, in percent?
body.explanation: Real policy rate ≈ 5.25% minus 5.0% = 0.25%. That is very low. Compare it with late 2025, when actual inflation was running near 1% and the repo rate measured against it was above 4%. With inflation projected to peak at 5.9% in October to December 2026, a real rate this thin is exactly why markets have stopped expecting further cuts.

children.text: Has Inflation Targeting Worked?

The RBI's own review compared inflation before and after the framework. Average inflation fell from 6.8% in the 2012 to 2016 period to 4.9% after targeting began, and inflation became less volatile, with its standard deviation dropping from 2.3 to 1.5 percentage points.

body.title: Annual Average CPI Inflation Under the Target (%)

children.text: The record is not perfect. Inflation touched or crossed the 6% ceiling in FY21 and FY23 as the pandemic and the war hit supply chains. But compare this chart with the near 10% inflation of the years just before targeting, and the difference in stability is clear.

body.title: Go Deeper: What Changed in the New CPI Series

children.text: In February 2026, MoSPI released a revised CPI with base year 2024. The update matters because the inflation target is measured on this index.

cells: 49 more goods and 10 more services added, including OTT subscriptions and online prices

children.text: A lower food weight means monsoon shocks move headline inflation a little less than before, which slightly strengthens the case for targeting headline CPI.

cards.definition: A framework where the central bank's main goal is an inflation target, while still keeping growth in mind.
The 2% to 6% range around India's 4% target. Staying outside it for three consecutive quarters counts as failure.
Inflation across the full CPI basket, including food and fuel. India's official target measure.
Inflation excluding food and fuel, which is more stable and more responsive to interest rates.
The RBI Act provision requiring a written report to the government when the inflation target is missed.
The nominal interest rate minus inflation. The true cost of borrowing and true return on saving.
When people believe inflation will stay near the target, which itself helps keep inflation stable.

body.label: MoSPI Consumer Price Index Page
body.description: The official source for each month's CPI release, usually published around the 12th of the following month.

body.title: Track Inflation Like the MPC Does
steps: Find the latest monthly CPI inflation print on the MoSPI website
Note whether it is above or below the 4% target, and by how much
Calculate the average of the last three months to get the quarterly figure
Subtract that inflation from the current repo rate of 5.25% to estimate the real rate
Compare the latest print with the RBI's projection of 5.9% for October to December 2026
Decide whether the next MPC move is more likely to be a hold, a cut or a hike, and write down why

points: India's inflation target is 4% headline CPI with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%, retained for April 2026 to March 2031.
The framework came from the 2014 Urjit Patel Committee and became law in 2016, after years of inflation near 10%.
India targets 4%, not 2%, because food carries a large CPI weight and a fast-growing economy sees faster price change.
Failure means average inflation outside the band for three consecutive quarters, which forces the RBI to explain itself in writing.
The RBI failed on the high side in 2022 and came within one quarter of failing on the low side in 2025-26.
Repo rate minus expected inflation gives the real policy rate, the quickest way to judge whether policy is tight or loose.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not investment advice. Inflation data and RBI projections are as of September 2026 and are revised over time.
